0.0.n: お adds politeness to 電話 in this standard telephone greeting.

0.1.n: Combines with ございます to make the thanks polite.

0.2.n: ござい is part of ございます, which makes ありがとう more polite.

0.3.n: ます completes the polite expression ありがとうございます.

1.0.n: メッシュ is the company name; 社 means company.

1.1.n: の links the company to Wang, showing affiliation.

1.2.n: 王 is the speaker’s surname here, not the word for king.

1.3.n: で begins でございます, a very polite equivalent of です.

1.4.n: ござい combines with で and ます to form the formal expression でございます.

1.5.n: ます completes でございます, used here for a formal self-introduction.

2.0.n: N is the company’s name here.

2.1.n: 株式会社 identifies the business as a stock company and forms part of its official name.

2.2.n: の connects Ishida to the company they represent.

2.3.n: 石田 is the speaker’s surname.

2.4.n: と marks the name being given before 申します.

2.5.n: 申します is the polite form of 申す, a humble way to say 言う when introducing yourself.

3.0.n: いつも describes the ongoing support acknowledged in this business greeting.

3.1.n: お adds politeness to 世話; the whole expression acknowledges help or an ongoing business relationship.

3.2.n: に marks the state entered with なる; お世話になる means to receive someone’s help.

3.3.n: なって is the て-form of なる; おります humbly replaces います to describe an ongoing situation.

4.0.n: N is the company’s name here.

4.1.n: 株式会社 forms part of the company’s official name.

4.2.n: の shows Ishida’s affiliation with N Corporation.

4.3.n: 石田 is a surname; 様 is a highly respectful title that does not specify gender.

4.4.n: で combines with いらっしゃいます to make a respectful equivalent of です.

4.5.n: With で, いらっしゃいます respectfully identifies the listener rather than describing their location.

4.6.n: ね asks the listener to confirm the identity just stated.

5.0.n: いつも emphasizes the continuing relationship acknowledged in this routine business greeting.

5.1.n: お adds politeness to 世話, used here to acknowledge the other party’s help.

5.2.n: に connects お世話 to なる as the state of receiving help.

5.3.n: なっております is a humble, formal version of なっています, describing an ongoing situation.

6.0.n: 部 means department; 総務 refers to general administrative affairs.

6.1.n: の links Inoue to their department.

6.2.n: 井上 is a surname; 様 adds strong respect without specifying gender.

6.3.n: は marks Inoue as the person whose presence is being asked about.

6.4.n: いらっしゃいます is a respectful form of います, used here to ask whether Inoue is present.

6.5.n: か turns the polite statement into a question.

7.0.n: 総務部 names the department where Inoue works.

7.1.n: の connects the department with Inoue.

7.2.n: 井上 is a surname; the employee omits 様 when referring to their own colleague to an outsider.

7.3.n: です makes this confirmation polite.

7.4.n: ね seeks confirmation that Inoue is the person the caller wants.

8.0.n: 少々 is a formal way to express a small amount of time.

8.1.n: お plus the stem of 待つ forms part of the polite request pattern お待ちいただく.

8.2.n: いただけます expresses receiving a favor as possible; でしょう adds indirectness, making the request especially deferential.

8.3.n: か completes the indirect, polite request.

0.tip: お電話ありがとうございます is a standard polite greeting when answering a business call.

1.tip: でございます is a very formal alternative to です, suitable for introducing yourself on a business call.

2.lit: N Corporation’s Ishida, I am called.
2.tip: Name + と申します is a humble, polite way to introduce yourself.

3.lit: Always, I have been receiving your care.
3.tip: This set business greeting expresses appreciation for an ongoing relationship, even without a specific recent favor.

4.lit: N Corporation’s honored Ishida you are, right?
4.tip: でいらっしゃいます respectfully identifies the other person, while ね requests confirmation.

5.lit: Always, I have been receiving your care.
5.tip: Repeating this greeting is a normal reciprocal courtesy in business conversations.

6.lit: General Affairs Department’s honored Inoue, as for, is present?
6.tip: いらっしゃいます respectfully replaces います when asking whether someone is there.

7.lit: General Affairs Department’s Inoue it is, right?
7.tip: When speaking to outsiders, Japanese employees normally omit respectful titles for their own colleagues.

8.lit: A moment, could I receive your waiting?
8.tip: お待ちいただけますでしょうか is an especially polite way to ask someone to wait or hold the line.
